title: Navigation for a B2B SaaS company
metaTitle: Navigation for a B2B SaaS company site
excerpt: Navigation should map jobs the buyer already has, in their words, with one path that books a demo. A list of departments makes them guess.
alt: A silver laptop open to a code editor on a white desk, with a monitor, mug, and phone behind it. The article is about a navigation bar that stays readable beside real work.
caption: The menu has to make sense on a desk that is already busy. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What belongs in a B2B SaaS header?
faqs.answer: Put the jobs a buyer has on the day they arrive. Seeing the product, the price, a proof, and booking a demo are enough for most companies, plus a quiet login. Department names such as solutions or resources make the buyer guess.

faqs.question: How should the demo appear in navigation?
faqs.answer: Use one label, such as book a demo, and keep it on every page. The click should land on a short path that matches the label, not a long essay. Do not hide that path inside a contact drawer.

faqs.question: Should the phone menu match the desktop bar?
faqs.answer: Write the phone list first. Items that only appear in a hover menu do not exist for many visitors. The demo should be visible when the menu opens, in the same words as the desktop action.

sources.title: Influencing title links in search results

markdown:
A B2B SaaS company website navigation is a map of jobs, not a list of departments. An operator who already runs software should see labels they already use, and one path that books a demo. If the header reads like an org chart, they will guess, and guessing is how a ready buyer ends up in a blog instead of a product.

Keep the map short enough to hold in memory. Product. Pricing. Proof. Book a demo. Login, if they have an account. Anything else has to win a place by being a job this buyer has on the day they arrive. A link that exists because a team wanted a homepage of its own is a tax on the header.

## Jobs, not an org chart

Departments name themselves. Solutions. Platform. Company. Resources. Those words describe how you are organized. They do not describe what the operator is trying to do. The operator is trying to see the product, judge the price, check a story, or talk to someone.

Rename the items as those jobs. "Product" can be the homepage or a page that shows the screen. "Pricing" should say pricing. "Customers" or "Proof" should point at a constraint and a decision, not at a magazine. "Book a demo" is a job with a verb. It should look like an action, not like another article.

Google's guidance on title links asks for titles that are clear and specific, because people and search both use the title to decide what a page is. Navigation is the same promise, one level up. The label and the title of the destination should agree. If the header says "Product" and the page title is a slogan, the map lied. Fix the title or fix the label. Do not ask the operator to reconcile them.

A dropdown can exist when there are two real destinations under one job. Pricing and a security note. Proof and a single case. A dropdown of twelve "solutions" by industry is the org chart again, wearing a menu. Collapse it until each item is a page you would be proud to open cold.

## Words they already use

Listen to the words in demos and support, and use those. If buyers say "the queue," do not label the page "workflow intelligence." If they say "seats," the pricing label should not say "plans and packages" unless that is truly their phrase.

Test a label by finishing the sentence "I need to…" The operator should be able to finish it without your help. I need to see the price. I need to see a team like mine. I need to book a demo. I need to log in. Labels that fail the sentence are labels for you.

Avoid two labels for one job. "Get started" and "Book a demo" and "Talk to sales" in the same header are one path wearing three names. Pick the true one. If self-serve and a demo are both real, they are different jobs and the labels should say so. "Start a workspace" and "Book a demo." The difference should be obvious before the click.

Login stays in the corner, quiet and spelled as login. It is a job for customers, not a campaign. Do not style it as the primary action. The primary action is for the person who cannot log in yet.

## One path that books a demo

One item in the header should book the demo. Give it a persistent treatment so it survives every page. The label stays the same on the homepage, the pricing page, and the proof page. Changing the verb per campaign makes the map feel unstable, and an unstable map feels like a company that is still deciding what it sells.

The path should land on a page or a scheduler that matches the label. If "Book a demo" opens a ten-field essay, the navigation overpromised. Land on a short confirmation of what the call is, with a way to pick a time. The header is not the place to qualify them. Qualification can happen in three fields after they have agreed to the job.

Do not hide the demo inside "Contact." Contact is a drawer. The operator has to open it to learn whether a demo lives there. Say demo if you mean demo. Save contact for a genuine alternate, and even then, consider whether the alternate deserves the header or only the footer.

On long pages, the header path is enough. A repeated button in the body can use the same label. A different label in the body splits the map. Consistency is the courtesy.

## What to drop from the header

Drop the blog, unless the blog is how this buyer buys, which it rarely is. The writing can live in the footer and still be findable. A header slot is expensive. Spend it on a job.

Drop careers, press, and the partner program from the first row. They are real pages for other people. The footer can carry them without asking every operator to step around them.

Drop a search box until the site is large enough that a person cannot see the map. On a short site, search is an admission that the labels failed. Fix the labels. Add search when there are many proof pages or many docs and the map cannot hold them.

Drop industry pages that repeat the homepage with a noun swapped. If you have a genuinely different job for a genuinely different buyer, give it a label that says the job. If the pages are the same screen with a new adjective, one page will do.

Count the items. Five is a comfortable ceiling for this kind of company, including the demo. Six can work. Nine means someone was being polite to a stakeholder. Politeness belongs in the meeting. The header belongs to the buyer.

When a stakeholder wants a link, give it a test week in the footer and see if anyone uses it. Promotion into the header should require a job you can name, not a compromise you are tired of discussing. A header built from compromises becomes a museum of old arguments. The operator does not know those arguments. They only know that the bar is hard to scan and the demo is one item among many. Make the demo easy to find, and let the museum close.

## The phone menu is the real menu

Most of these buyers will open the site on a phone between meetings. The desktop bar is not the menu they meet. The list behind the menu button is. Write that list first. If an item only makes sense in a hover dropdown, it does not exist for them.

Order the phone list by the job sequence. See the product. See the price. See a proof. Book a demo. Login last or first, but not lost in the middle of marketing links. The demo should be visible without a second tap into a parent called company.

Keep the menu short enough that the demo is on screen when the menu opens. A phone menu that scrolls for a screen and a half has reintroduced the org chart. Cut until the action is in view.

Do not rely on a hamburger icon with no word. A visible "Menu" next to the demo action is kinder. The operator should not have to interpret an icon to find the price. Icons are fine beside words. They are a poor substitute for them.

## How to test the labels

Ask three people who match the buyer, and who did not name the menu, to do four tasks out loud. Find what the product does. Find the price. Find a team like theirs. Book a demo. Watch where they hesitate. Hesitation is a bad label, even if they eventually succeed.

If they say "I guess it's under resources," the label is wrong. Move the page. Rename it. Do not add a tooltip to explain a header. A header that needs a tooltip has already failed.

Check the path with a keyboard. A menu that only opens on hover is a menu some people cannot use. W3C's WCAG overview sets the expectation that the interface can be operated, not only looked at. A demo path that depends on a fine hover is a path you will lose in a screen reader and on a phone. Click or tap should open it. Escape should close it. The focused item should be visible.

Read every label next to the title of its page. Disagreement is a defect. Fix it before you debate the typeface of the bar.

## The footer is not a second homepage

The footer can hold the quiet pages. Careers. Privacy. A status page. The writing. A way to email if that is a real door. It should still use job words. It should not become a dump of every URL you have ever published, in three columns of equal gray.

Repeat the demo once in the footer for the person who scrolled. Same label. Same destination. A footer that introduces a new offer the header never mentioned is a second strategy. Pick one map.

When the labels are doing their job, the pictures have to argue the same jobs. A header that says the product, sitting over a stock photograph of a lobby, splits the company in two. Read [how to direct photographs so they show the product in use](/blog/photography-direction-for-a-b2b-saas-company) before you fill the page with a mood the menu did not promise.

If you want to walk a header against the jobs a buyer actually has, book [an intro call](https://cal.com/hanabi/30min). Bring the current labels. The useful work is deciding which five deserve the bar.
